title: Predictive Analytics
shortDefinition: The use of historical data and statistical models to forecast future outcomes or behaviors.
definition: Predictive analytics is the use of historical data, statistical algorithms, and machine learning techniques to forecast future outcomes or behaviors — answering 'what's likely to happen next' rather than simply describing what has already happened. Predictive analytics powers demand forecasting, churn prediction, credit risk scoring, and maintenance scheduling across virtually every industry.

sections.title: Predictive vs. descriptive vs. prescriptive analytics
sections.description: Descriptive summarizes the past; predictive forecasts the future; prescriptive recommends actions.

content.text: Descriptive analytics summarizes what has already happened (last quarter's sales by region). Predictive analytics forecasts what's likely to happen next (next quarter's expected sales based on historical patterns and current trends). Prescriptive analytics goes a step further, recommending specific actions to take based on those predictions (which customers to target with retention offers based on predicted churn risk). Most business value comes from combining all three — understanding the past, forecasting the future, and acting on that forecast.

sections.title: Why predictive models need validation, not just deployment

content.text: A predictive model's value depends entirely on whether its forecasts are actually reliable enough to inform real business decisions — a model that 'predicts' with high confidence but poor real-world accuracy can lead to worse decisions than no forecast at all. Rigorous predictive analytics requires validating accuracy against historical holdout data before deployment, and ongoing monitoring for model drift as the underlying patterns the model was trained on shift over time.

items: Validation against holdout data — test accuracy on data not used for training.
Model drift monitoring — track performance degradation over time.
Confidence calibration — ensure predicted probabilities match actual outcomes.
Business impact validation — does the forecast actually improve decisions?
Ongoing evaluation — regular accuracy checks against current data.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of predictive analytics

content.text: Predictive analytics has significant limitations. Models are only as good as the historical data they're trained on — poor data quality leads to poor predictions. Forecasts are probabilistic, not certain, and can give false confidence if not properly calibrated. Predictive models can degrade over time as underlying patterns shift, and they can amplify biases present in historical data. Over-reliance on predictions without human judgment can lead to poor business decisions.

items: Data dependency: predictions are only as good as the training data.
Probabilistic nature: forecasts are uncertain, not deterministic.
False confidence: models can appear more reliable than they are.
Drift: model performance degrades as patterns change over time.
Bias amplification: models can amplify historical biases.
Over-reliance: predictions should inform, not replace, human judgment.
Garbage in, garbage out: poor data quality leads to poor forecasts.

content.title: Important
content.text: Predictive models are tools to inform decisions, not replace them. Always combine forecasts with human judgment and domain expertise.

sections.title: Best practices for predictive analytics implementation

content.text: Building effective predictive analytics requires careful data preparation, model validation, and ongoing monitoring. The following practices can help ensure your predictive models deliver reliable forecasts.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Start with a clear business question — what forecast will inform a specific decision?
Collect and clean historical data relevant to the prediction target.
Split data into training, validation, and holdout test sets.
Start with a simple baseline before more complex models.
Validate accuracy on holdout data — not just training or validation data.
Implement explainability tooling for consequential models.
Monitor for drift and retrain based on measured degradation.
Combine predictions with human judgment in decision-making.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure forecast accuracy on holdout data — the true test of a predictive model is how well it performs on data it wasn't trained on.

items.question: What's the difference between predictive and descriptive analytics?
items.answer: Descriptive analytics summarizes past data; predictive analytics forecasts future outcomes based on that data using statistical and machine learning models.

items.question: What industries use predictive analytics?
items.answer: Predictive analytics is used across virtually every industry: retail (demand forecasting), finance (credit risk), healthcare (patient outcomes), manufacturing (maintenance prediction), marketing (churn prediction), and logistics (route optimization).

items.question: What is the difference between forecasting and predictive analytics?
items.answer: Forecasting is a specific type of predictive analytics focused on time-series predictions (e.g., sales next month). Predictive analytics is the broader field that includes classification (e.g., will this customer churn?) and regression (e.g., what will their lifetime value be?).

items.question: What are common predictive analytics algorithms?
items.answer: Common algorithms include linear regression, logistic regression, random forests, gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM), and neural networks. The right choice depends on your data type, prediction target, and interpretability needs.

items.question: How do you handle seasonality in predictive analytics?
items.answer: Seasonality (e.g., holiday sales spikes) must be accounted for in forecasting models. Common approaches include seasonal decomposition, including seasonal features, and using models designed for seasonal data like SARIMA or Prophet.
